S021.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
S021.description: Symptoms where speech or thought appears scattered and difficult to follow due to a lack of logical or consistent flow.

subtypes.Derailment or Loose Associations: A speech pattern of switching rapidly from one topic to another with no logical connection between thoughts.
subtypes.Tangentiality: Speech that deviates entirely from the question and fails to answer directly.
subtypes.Incoherence or Word Salad: Severe fragmentation of speech and sentence structure, making it nearly impossible to understand.
subtypes.Neologisms: Using made-up words that have meaning only to the individual.
subtypes.Clang Associations: Speech governed by sounds, such as rhyming, rather than the meaning of words.

S022.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
S022.description: A state where behavior and motor control are severely disturbed, appearing as movements or reactions inappropriate to the situation.

subtypes.Childlike Silliness: Inappropriate, childish, or illogical behavior appearing in situations.
subtypes.Stupor: No psychomotor activity; not actively relating to environment.
subtypes.Catalepsy: Passive induction of a posture held against gravity.
subtypes.Waxy Flexibility: Slight, even resistance to positioning by examiner.
subtypes.Mutism: No, or very little, verbal response despite the ability to speak.
subtypes.Negativism: Opposition or no response to instructions or external stimuli without apparent motive.
subtypes.Posturing: Spontaneous and active maintenance of a posture against gravity.
subtypes.Mannerism: Odd, circumstantial caricature of normal actions.
subtypes.Agitation: Excessive motor activity without obvious external cause.
subtypes.Grimacing: Contorted facial expressions irrelevant to the situation.

symptom.disease_info: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking and behavior, and negative symptoms such as diminished emotional expression and social withdrawal, with at least six months of disturbance and one month of active-phase symptoms. It typically emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood, but late-onset cases can occur, particularly in women and under medical or psychosocial stress. The course is often relapsing and remitting with variable functional decline, and impairment in work, relationships, or self-care is required for diagnosis. It is distinguished from mood disorders with psychotic features by the persistence of psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes and from brief or schizophreniform psychoses by its longer duration and broader impact on functioning.

patient.stressor: Richard’s difficulties started after he left his community college program and took on full-time warehouse work, moving from the predictable structure of school and part-time shifts into rotating schedules and heavier responsibilities. At first his supervisors appreciated his meticulous style, but over the ensuing 11 months he became increasingly unable to maintain orderly routines, with coworkers noticing abrupt changes in how he organized pallets, followed safety procedures, and interacted during shift briefings. His family saw a stark contrast between the careful planner who once managed fishing trips and woodworking projects down to the last detail and the young man who now seemed unable to stick to basic plans or behave in ways that fit the situation at church and at home. When mounting problems at work led to a formal performance warning and his pastor mentioned being concerned about how disorganized and out of step he seemed during volunteer shifts, his parents brought him to psychiatric services for an urgent evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to keep my actions in order at work—I start doing things that don’t fit what I’m supposed to be doing and everything just turns into a mess.”

S021.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
S021.description: Symptoms where speech or thought appears scattered and difficult to follow due to a lack of logical or consistent flow.
S021.manifestation: When people at work or my parents ask me a simple question, like what I did on my last shift, I start talking about the pallets, then jump to a story about fishing with my uncle, then remember something about the safety video and I just keep going off in different directions until I can see on their faces that they have no idea what I’m talking about—even I lose track of what I was trying to say in the first place.

S022.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
S022.description: A state where behavior and motor control are severely disturbed, appearing as movements or reactions inappropriate to the situation.
S022.manifestation: On the floor I’ll suddenly stop in the middle of moving a pallet and just stand there holding the jack in a weird way or start re-stacking boxes that were already fine, or I’ll pace up and down the aisle waving my hands or making faces without really knowing why, even when my supervisor is telling me to knock it off and get back to the actual job.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: Because of how mixed up I get, my boss wrote me up for poor performance, my hours have been cut back, and even at church and at home people avoid putting me in charge of things because I can’t follow through the way I used to.
add_requirements.duration: All of this has been going on ever since I left community college for the full-time warehouse job, which has been close to a year now.
add_requirements.psychotic_symptoms_duration: The really out-of-place actions and confused way of talking have been a constant problem for about the last six months or so.
